- Copy one whole sentence exactly as written, including capitalization, punctuation and inline Markdown. Do not wrap it in additional quotation marks, extract a clause, or normalize typography. Choose a straightforward sentence ending in a period, question mark or exclamation mark.
- Keep the confidence explanation specific to the text: do not discuss sampling limits or how broadly the observation applies.

Sample text:
---
The Museum of Small Things

This morning I found a receipt in the pocket of a winter coat: one orange, one loaf of bread, a candle shaped like a pear. The date had faded into a blue smudge, but I remembered the day anyway—or thought I did. Memory is a poor archivist. It keeps the ticket stub and loses the film. Still, I stood by the window with the receipt in my hand and felt the whole afternoon come back: the cold air sharp as a clean knife, the bakery steaming like a small, honest engine, the candle that never got lit because it looked too much like a fruit to burn.

I have been thinking about small things lately. Not small in the sense of unimportant, but small in the sense that they fit in the palm. A key. A stone. A sentence someone says and then forgets. The way a stranger on the bus held her umbrella with both hands as if it might try to escape. These are the objects and gestures that make up a life, though we rarely put them on display. We save the big moments in albums and the little ones in our bodies, where they wait like seeds.

On my walk to the corner store, I passed a man watering a single plant in a cracked pot. He was very serious about it. The water fell in a thin silver thread, and the plant—some kind of fern, maybe—looked no better or worse for the attention. But the man’s face had the concentration of a watchmaker. I wanted to tell him that I understood. That sometimes the only way to keep the world from spinning too fast is to water one small thing and watch the water disappear into the dirt.

The corner store smelled of cardboard and oranges. The woman behind the counter was reading a paperback with a broken spine. She didn’t look up when I came in, and I appreciated that. There is a kind of trust in not being watched. I bought milk and a chocolate bar I didn’t need and a lemon because it was the color of a good mood. Outside, the sky was doing that thing it does in early spring—gray, then silver, then almost blue—as if it can’t decide whether to apologize or start over.

I used to think that meaning arrived in loud rooms. Now I think it arrives in kitchens at night, when the dishwasher is humming and someone has left a spoon on the counter and the clock is ticking like a small, patient animal. My mother used to leave her teacup in the sink with a little tea still in it. I would find it in the morning, a dark ring at the bottom, and know she had been there, awake before me, thinking her private thoughts. That ring was a kind of message. Not a sentence, exactly. More like a proof of presence.

There is a word I like: “petrichor.” The smell of rain on dry ground. I like it not because it is beautiful—though it is—but because it names something we would otherwise have to point at and say, “You know, that smell.” Language is full of these small rescues. It reaches down and pulls a feeling out of the mud and gives it a little name tag. Most of the time we forget the names. But sometimes, on a walk, the air changes, and the word surfaces like a fish, and for a second the world is more specific than it was before.

At the end of my street there is a bench that nobody sits on. It faces a wall. I have decided it is a bench for thinking about walls. Once I saw a pigeon land on its back and stay there for a long time, doing nothing. Pigeons are excellent at doing nothing. They have mastered the art of being a small gray thought in a loud city. I envy them a little. I envy anyone who can sit still without feeling that stillness is a debt they will have to pay back later.

Tonight I will make soup. I will chop an onion and cry, and it will be a small, ordinary ceremony. I will listen to the radio and miss half of what is said and think about the receipt in my pocket and the man watering his fern and the woman with her paperback and the lemon on the counter, bright as a tiny sun. The world will keep doing what it does—breaking and mending, forgetting and remembering—and I will be here, in the middle of it, paying attention to the small things. Not because they are all I can manage. Because they are, in the end, the things that hold the whole thing together. A key. A stone. A sentence. A candle shaped like a pear.
---
